T H A R R O S / C A N A D A Data Note · TC-2026-001

Analytical Report: Traffic Collisions by
Location 2017-2024 (excluding 2023)
By Magnus Abdelnour
Published September 16, 2026 · Tharros Canada · tharros.ca/research/id/TC-2026-001
Overview
Published August 14, 2026, Traffic Collisions by Location 2017-2024 (excluding 2023) is a
dataset collected and maintained by the City of Ottawa, provided to the public under the
Open Data Licence Version 2.0, detailing all traffic collisions between 2017-2024 (excluding
2023) in the Ottawa region.1 A total of 94,406 traffic incidents were documented. Collision
information is collected via motor vehicle collision reports submitted by the Ottawa police
and provided to the city for inclusion in its collision database.2 This dataset provides
collision information, including the severity and number of victims, aiding city planning
officials in making educated decisions in relation to road policy changes or additions to
certain roads and routes to prevent future collisions.
Technical Contents
Each incident entry contains the incident’s date, exact coordinates, year, intersection/road
the incident occurred on, accident classification, impact type, road surface condition,
environmental condition, light/time of day, and traffic control (Figure 1). Furthermore, it
contains data on the number of vehicles, pedestrians, bicycles, motorcycles involved, as
well as injuries and the level of severity from minimal to fatal. This dataset is updated and
reviewed annually and has its metadata readily available. However, I found no separate data
dictionary or methodological guide.3 The data can be accessed online through the City of
Ottawa website, and can be viewed in three different forms: an embedded Geo-map, a
Tabular Data View or an ArcGIS Feature Layer. It can be accessed and downloaded/shared
via CSV, Shapefile, GeoJSON, and KML. Downloading the data via CSV was the most
efficient method; after the small pop-up window that appears when the download button is

pressed, I was able to open the table in Excel. The dataset is provided under the City of
Ottawa Open Data Licence Version 2.0, which allows copying, modification, publication
and commercial use as long as it’s for lawful purposes with proper attribution and
accreditation. 4
Quality & Limitations
The dataset provides detailed information on 94,406 reported traffic collisions across
Ottawa from 2017 to 2024 (excluding 2023). It uses official police collision reports and City
validation procedures, providing a strong basis for reliability and transparency. The data is
clearly structured and can be filtered by variables such as location, collision type and injury
severity, making it accessible for a wide range of analyses. However, the complete absence
of 2023 creates a significant gap and limits the dataset’s usefulness for continuous 2017 to
2024 trend analysis.
Fit for Use Assessment
This dataset is fit to be used for needs pertaining to geographic distribution, characteristics,
and trends in reported traffic collisions in the City of Ottawa. While the dataset is well
suited for identifying broader collision trends across Ottawa, the absence of 2023 limits its
reliability for continuous analysis and weakens any findings and conclusions that depend
on complete 2017 to 2024 comparisons.

T H A R R O S / C A N A D A Research Report · TC-2026-002
Canada Inside SAFE: What Access to
Europe’s €150B Defence Initiative Has
Cost, and Who’s Gained So Far
By Magnus Abdelnour
Published September 24, 2026 · Tharros Canada · tharros.ca/research/id/TC-2026-002
Overview
What does a European military and defence loan procurement program have to do with Canada?
What does it mean for Canadians now that Canada has joined? This report will aim to analyse what
access to Europe’s €150B defence loans has cost, and who’s gained so far across Canadian
industries. On December 1, 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the conclusion of
negotiations for Canada’s participation in SAFE.1 This opened the EU up to €150 billion to invest in
defence contracts from Canadian firms. As per Mark Carney’s statement, it “opens massive new
opportunities for Canadian manufacturers to build and export Canadian-made technologies and
capabilities.”2 However, nine months on, it is now time to analyse just how effective this agreement
has been, and if it truly has opened massive new opportunities for Canadian manufacturers.
The Agreement
Under the agreement between the European Union and Canada concerning participation under the
SAFE Instrument,3 Canadian firms are provided with preferential treatment and access to defence
procurements financed by the SAFE initiative. In return, the Canadian government was required to
provide financial contributions commensurate to a portion of the value Canadian firms receive from
their contracts, received under the SAFE instrument.4
Key components of the agreement are as follows: Under the agreement, Canadian firms are allowed
to make up 80% of the total value of any procurement made through SAFE, a significant step up from
the 35% threshold third-party nations are subject to. The Canadian government was to provide a €10
million financial contribution, of which €7.5 million was to be treated as a down payment and credit
towards Canada’s future participation. Canada is to remit a participation fee equal to 15% of the
total value of the Canadian content in any SAFE procurement where European content makes up
65% or less of the total contract. Under the agreement, Canadian firms are to be treated on the same

December 1, 2025, https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2025/12/01/prime-minister-carney-secures-canadas-participation-
european-unions.
2 Prime Minister of Canada, “Prime Minister Carney Secures Canada’s Participation.”
3 Global Affairs Canada, “Agreement between the European Union and Canada Concerning Participation under the SAFE Instrument,”
modified February 24, 2026, https://www.international.gc.ca/world-monde/international_relations-relations_internationales/eu-
ue/agreement-accord.aspx?lang=eng.
4 Global Affairs Canada, “Agreement between the European Union and Canada.”

footing as European firms, ensuring non-discriminatory access to opportunities.5 In theory, if a
Canadian firm completes a €100M contract with 50% Canadian content, coming in under the 65%
European content rule, the Canadian government would owe 15% of €50M, equaling a €7.5 million
bill, as the Canadian government is only subject to paying the fee on the 50% input that the Canadian
firm provided.
Compared to the United Kingdom’s non-integrated status, Canada’s participation offers many
potential gains.

The United Kingdom’s limited ability to operate within SAFE, and the EU’s defence procurement
initiative as laid out above, show the extent to which this Canadian agreement could benefit
Canadian industry.6
Who has gained so far?
Across Canadian industries and available data, over the past nine months, only one Canadian firm
has been awarded a contract through SAFE. The Montreal-based Canadian firm Marconi
Technologies is contracted to fulfil an order worth over C$10 million, building ORION tactical radios
for the Polish Cyber Command, to be fulfilled over 2026 to 2030.7 This was announced by Prime
Minister Mark Carney in a news release on 17 June 2026. However, three months since the
announcement in June, the government has made no further announcements surrounding new
contracts through SAFE. Much of the procurement details and decision-making are confidential and

Under the SAFE initiative, eligible purchases are sorted into two categories.8 Category 1: Ammunition
and missile, artillery, small drones and counter-drone systems, critical infrastructure protection,
cyber, military mobility. Category 2: Air and missile defence, larger drones, strategic enablers, space
asset protection, AI and electronic warfare. Any future contracts awarded to Canadian firms through
SAFE will need to fall within these two categories.
How much does Canada have to gain?
To understand how much Canada has to gain, we first look at the existing demand for Canadian
military and defence goods. The tables below show Canadian military exports by region and across
Europe from 2024–2025, as well as the wider defence industry’s exports from 2022–2024, per Global
Affairs Canada and the Canadian government’s State of Canada’s Defence Industry Report: Spring

These tables demonstrate the existing state of the European and Global demand for Canadian
military and defence goods. The Canadian government has yet to post the 2026 export numbers;
however, if we extrapolate on the already present data it would be reasonable to assume that the
demand for Canadian military goods has increased due to recent political pressures from a shrinking
American presence and reliability in the EU, and may be further spurred by the SAFE agreement. To
put this into perspective, around €140 billion of SAFE funding is yet to be spent through 2030, while
Canadian military exports to the EU-27 totalled C$898.5 million in 2025. Even 1% of the remaining
SAFE funds would be worth more than double Canada’s 2025 military exports to the EU.
What this report cannot show
While this report try’s to give a clear image of Canada’s role in SAFE so far, there are limits to what the
available data can show. Neither the European Commission or the Canadian government has

published a full list of contracts awarded under SAFE, so Canadian contracts may exist that are yet to
be made public. The 15% participation fee is not calculated until March 2027, meaning we cannot yet
say what Canada will pay beyond the initial €10 million. Furthermore, the export data in Tables 1 to 3
comes from before the first SAFE loans were paid out in May 2026, so it shows demand for Canadian
exports rather than the effect of SAFE itself. The search of the EU’s TED portal has its own short
comings, as it only picks up notices that mention SAFE directly, and many contracts are never
publicly advertised.
Conclusion
By all accounts, the results of this research all point towards one conclusion. It is far too soon to form
a conclusive view of the effectiveness of Canada’s participation in the European Union’s SAFE
initiative, as neither governing body, Canadian nor European, has published sufficient data.
Furthermore, of the 30 SAFE-linked contract awards published on the EU’s TED portal as of
September 2026, none lists a Canadian winner. Canada’s one confirmed award, Marconi’s Polish
contract, was announced by the Prime Minister and does not appear in the EUs TED portal, which
suggests most SAFE contracts are not publicly advertised.13 The table below sets out this evidence:
